views.name: job_postings_with_company
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  j.job_id,
  j.company_id,
  j.job_title_short,
  j.job_title,
  j.job_location,
  j.job_via,
  j.job_schedule_type,
  j.job_work_from_home,
  j.search_location,
  j.job_posted_date,
  j.job_no_degree_mention,
  j.job_health_insurance,
  j.job_country,
  j.salary_rate,
  j.salary_year_avg,
  j.salary_hour_avg,
  c.name AS name,
  c.link AS link,
  c.link_google AS link_google,
  c.thumbnail AS thumbnail
FROM job_postings_fact AS j
LEFT JOIN job_company AS c
  ON j.company_id = c.company_id

params.description: Row-level view of job postings enriched with company attributes; answers questions about individual job postings and their associated company metadata.
params.when_to_use: Retrieve attributes for a specific job posting (by job_id) together with its company info. | Produce a list of job postings with company name/link/thumbnail for display or downstream per-job analytics. | Filter or segment job postings by posting date, location, salary fields, or company attributes while preserving one-row-per-job grain.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to compute aggregated metrics (counts, distinct counts, averages) over jobs without performing explicit aggregation — the view is at job_id grain, so naive joins to one-to-many tables and then counting rows will double-count. | Do not join this view directly to any one-to-many detail (e.g., job_skills_exploded) and then assume measures (one-per-job) remain accurate — such joins will multiply rows per job and silently inflate counts/averages unless you pre-aggregate the many-side. | Do not use this view to represent company-level aggregates (e.g., number of jobs per company) without grouping by company_id because this view contains multiple rows per company and would produce incorrect cohort-level results if treated as company-grain.
params.output_schema: job_id: unique identifier of the job posting — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_id | company_id: identifier of the employer associated with the job — sourced from job_postings_fact.company_id | job_title_short: short title text for the job posting — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_title_short | job_title: full job title text for the job posting — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_title | job_location: textual location field for the job (as stored on the posting) — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_location | job_via: source attribution or via-field for the posting (e.g., posted via) — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_via | job_schedule_type: schedule classification (e.g., full-time/part-time) — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_schedule_type | job_work_from_home: indicator/flag describing remote/work-from-home allowance — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_work_from_home | search_location: normalized/derived search location associated with the posting — sourced from job_postings_fact.search_location | job_posted_date: date (or datetime) when the job was posted — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_posted_date | job_no_degree_mention: boolean/flag indicating whether the posting mentions no degree requirement — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_no_degree_mention | job_health_insurance: boolean/flag indicating whether health insurance is mentioned — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_health_insurance | job_country: country code or name for the job posting — sourced from job_postings_fact.job_country | salary_rate: salary rate type or currency/period indicator as stored (e.g., 'yearly'/'hourly') — sourced from job_postings_fact.salary_rate | salary_year_avg: average/normalized yearly salary field for the posting (as stored) — sourced from job_postings_fact.salary_year_avg | salary_hour_avg: average hourly salary field for the posting (as stored) — sourced from job_postings_fact.salary_hour_avg | name: company name for the associated company — sourced from job_company.name | link: company website/link as stored in company table — sourced from job_company.link | link_google: company Google profile link (if present) — sourced from job_company.link_google | thumbnail: company thumbnail or logo URL/path — sourced from job_company.thumbnail
params.grounded_columns: job_postings_fact.job_id | job_postings_fact.company_id | job_postings_fact.job_title_short | job_postings_fact.job_title | job_postings_fact.job_location | job_postings_fact.job_via | job_postings_fact.job_schedule_type | job_postings_fact.job_work_from_home | job_postings_fact.search_location | job_postings_fact.job_posted_date | job_postings_fact.job_no_degree_mention | job_postings_fact.job_health_insurance | job_postings_fact.job_country | job_postings_fact.salary_rate | job_postings_fact.salary_year_avg | job_postings_fact.salary_hour_avg | job_company.company_id | job_company.name | job_company.link | job_company.link_google | job_company.thumbnail
params.metric: This view contains no aggregated metrics by itself; all output columns are direct projections or renames of source columns. | salary_year_avg = job_postings_fact.salary_year_avg  -- stored normalized per job (not computed here) | salary_hour_avg = job_postings_fact.salary_hour_avg  -- stored normalized per job (not computed here)
params.composition: Safe: join this view to dimension/lookups that are one-row-per-key: e.g., join to a precomputed company-level aggregate on company_id (company_agg) — safe because company_agg must be one-row-per-company and will not multiply job rows. | Safe: join to date/calendar dimension on job_posted_date to enrich posting dates — calendar dims are typically one-row-per-date and will not duplicate rows. | Not safe: do NOT directly join to job_skills_exploded (one-to-many: job_id -> multiple skills) without pre-aggregation; joining will produce multiple rows per job and duplicate job-level attributes and any downstream counts/averages unless you use DISTINCT or aggregate the skills first (for example aggregate skills to a comma-delimited string or count per job before joining). | Not safe: do NOT join to legislators_profile or other sibling JOIN views that are many-to-many to job_postings_fact without verifying join cardinality. Any join that can return multiple rows per job_id will multiply this view's rows. | Guidance: when you need to combine one-row-per-job measures with many-side details, either (a) aggregate the many-side to one-row-per-job first, then join, or (b) join and immediately GROUP BY job_id and re-compute measures (e.g., use MIN/MAX/AVG with care) to restore correct job-level grain.
params.comparison: Use job_postings_salary_rank instead when you need salary-relative ranking or percentile within a partition — that sibling is a RANK view intended for salary ordering, whereas this view only surfaces raw salary fields. | Use job_skills_exploded when you need one-row-per-(job,skill) for skill-level analysis — job_postings_with_company is one-row-per-job and will hide multiple skills unless you explode or join appropriately with aggregation. | Use cities_with_country or cities_population_by_country when your primary join key or analysis is city-level; this view contains job_location and job_country but is not a city-level aggregate, so city-level metrics should be derived by grouping this view or by joining to those city-level sibling views depending on whether you need aggregated population/context.

views.description: Denormalized job postings enriched with company metadata. Use when answering questions that need job attributes together with company name/link/thumbnail (e.g., salary by company, counts by company, location distributions). | Use for: Top companies by number of job postings; Average salary by company or company name; Job distribution by company and location; Identify companies offering remote work or health insurance

views.name: job_skills_exploded
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  j.job_id,
  j.company_id,
  j.job_title_short,
  j.job_title,
  j.job_location,
  j.job_posted_date,
  s.skill_id,
  d.skills AS skills,
  d.type AS type
FROM job_postings_fact AS j
JOIN skills_job_dim AS s
  ON j.job_id = s.job_id
LEFT JOIN skills_dim AS d
  ON s.skill_id = d.skill_id

params.description: A row-level exploded view of skills attached to each job posting: one row per (job_id, skill_id) pairing including job metadata and the skill attributes.
params.when_to_use: List all skills for each job posting (e.g., enumerate skills for a job detail page). | Filter or aggregate skills at the job-skill grain (e.g., count skills per job). | Join job-level attributes to skill attributes when the desired result should preserve one row per job-skill pair.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view into another dataset and then summing job-level metrics without re-aggregating — because the view is exploded to one row per skill and will multiply job-level measures if naively aggregated at job or company grain. | Using it to produce one-row-per-job outputs (e.g., job counts by company) without deduplicating job_id first — doing so will overcount jobs that have multiple skills. | Treating it as a skills dictionary alone — it contains job-specific skill occurrences; use skills_dim for the canonical skill list instead.
params.output_schema: job_id: job_postings_fact.job_id — unique identifier of the job posting (part of this view's grain). | company_id: job_postings_fact.company_id — company that posted the job (job-level attribute). | job_title_short: job_postings_fact.job_title_short — short form of the job title (job-level attribute). | job_title: job_postings_fact.job_title — full job title (job-level attribute). | job_location: job_postings_fact.job_location — location text for the job (job-level attribute). | job_posted_date: job_postings_fact.job_posted_date — when the job was posted (job-level attribute). | skill_id: skills_job_dim.skill_id — identifier of the skill associated to the job (part of this view's grain). | skills: skills_dim.skills — human-readable skill name/label from the skills dimension (nullable because LEFT JOIN). | type: skills_dim.type — skill type/category from the skills dimension (nullable because LEFT JOIN).
params.grounded_columns: job_postings_fact.job_id | job_postings_fact.company_id | job_postings_fact.job_title_short | job_postings_fact.job_title | job_postings_fact.job_location | job_postings_fact.job_posted_date | skills_job_dim.skill_id | skills_dim.skills | skills_dim.type
params.metric: This view contains no derived aggregate metrics — all outputs are direct column projections from base tables. | If you need "skills_per_job = COUNT(skill_id)", compute it as a separate aggregation: skills_per_job = COUNT(skill_id) GROUP BY job_id from this view.
params.composition: Safe to join (cardinality-safe) to one-row-per-company or one-row-per-job views on company_id or job_id respectively, provided the target side is at most one row per join key: |  - Join to job_postings_with_company on job_id: safe because job_postings_with_company is expected to be one row per job_id (no duplication) — job-level attributes will not be multiplied. |  - Join to cities_with_country on job_location (if job_location is a city key and cities_with_country is one row per city): safe, because it will not multiply rows for the same job-skill pair. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables/views without re-aggregation, because this view is already at (job_id, skill_id) granularity and an extra one-to-many join will multiply rows and distort counts/metrics: |  - Do NOT join to a hypothetical job_applications_fact (many applications per job) without aggregating applications to job_id first — otherwise job-level counts (e.g., application_count) will be repeated per skill and over-counted. |  - Do NOT join to aliens_favorites_agg or cities_population_by_country if those siblings are at a finer grain that creates many rows per join key unless you first aggregate them to the join key. | When composing with aggregates, either aggregate this view up to the desired grain (e.g., GROUP BY job_id to get job-level measures) or aggregate the other side to match this view's (job_id, skill_id) grain.
params.comparison: Use job_postings_with_company instead when you need one row per job with company enrichment — it is the correct sibling when your target grain is job (not job-skill). | Use skills_dim when you need the canonical list of skills independent of job occurrences — skills_dim contains skill metadata without being tied to job occurrences. | Use cities_with_country when your analysis is focused on city-country mapping (not job-skill pairs); prefer that view if you only need location normalization and one row per city. | Do NOT substitute this view for aggregated sibling views like cities_population_by_country or aliens_favorites_agg — those are pre-aggregated and intended for different grains/metrics.

views.description: Jobs joined to skill labels via the bridge table to expose skill text for each job. Use for skill-based aggregations, searching jobs requiring certain skills, or counting jobs per skill. | Use for: Count jobs requiring a given skill; Top skills by job count; Average salary for jobs requiring a particular skill

views.name: cities_with_country
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.city_id,
  c.city_name,
  c.latitude,
  c.longitude,
  c.country_code_2,
  c.capital,
  c.population,
  c.insert_date,
  ct.country_id AS country_id,
  ct.country_name AS country_name,
  ct.country_code_3 AS country_code_3,
  ct.region AS region,
  ct.sub_region AS sub_region,
  ct.intermediate_region AS intermediate_region
FROM cities AS c
LEFT JOIN cities_countries AS ct
  ON c.country_code_2 = ct.country_code_2

params.description: Provides one row per city (grain: city_id) with city attributes and the matched country attributes via country_code_2.
params.when_to_use: Look up city-level attributes (name, coordinates, population, capital flag, insert_date) together with country-level metadata (country_id, country_name, country_code_3, region, sub_region, intermediate_region) for reporting, filtering, or joining when you need exactly one row per city. | Build maps, location lists, or city directories that need both city and country descriptive fields. | Filter or aggregate by country fields after ensuring aggregation is done at the city level (for example: count cities per country).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to compute country-level aggregates (e.g., total population per country) without re-aggregating at the country grain first — using this view directly to SUM(population) is acceptable only if you intend to sum city populations; it will undercount/overcount if city rows are duplicated by subsequent joins. | Do not join this view directly to one-to-many detail tables (for example: job_postings) expecting measures on the detail to remain accurate unless you account for duplication — joining a city-level row to many job_posting rows will multiply any city-level measures if they are later aggregated incorrectly. | Avoid using this view to represent a country-level entity or to deduplicate countries — multiple cities map to the same country, so treating it as unique per country is incorrect.
params.output_schema: city_id: Unique identifier for the city; derived from cities.city_id. | city_name: Human-readable name of the city; derived from cities.city_name. | latitude: City's latitude coordinate; derived from cities.latitude. | longitude: City's longitude coordinate; derived from cities.longitude. | country_code_2: Two-letter ISO country code associated with the city; derived from cities.country_code_2. | capital: Boolean/flag indicating whether the city is a capital (as stored); derived from cities.capital. | population: Population value for the city (as stored in cities); derived from cities.population. | insert_date: The insert_date timestamp for the city row; derived from cities.insert_date. | country_id: Country primary identifier from the countries reference table; derived from cities_countries.country_id (aliased ct.country_id). | country_name: Country name from reference table; derived from cities_countries.country_name (ct.country_name). | country_code_3: Three-letter ISO country code from reference table; derived from cities_countries.country_code_3 (ct.country_code_3). | region: Top-level region field from country reference; derived from cities_countries.region (ct.region). | sub_region: Sub-region field from country reference; derived from cities_countries.sub_region (ct.sub_region). | intermediate_region: Intermediate region field from country reference; derived from cities_countries.intermediate_region (ct.intermediate_region).
params.grounded_columns: cities.city_id | cities.city_name | cities.latitude | cities.longitude | cities.country_code_2 | cities.capital | cities.population | cities.insert_date | cities_countries.country_id | cities_countries.country_name | cities_countries.country_code_3 | cities_countries.region | cities_countries.sub_region | cities_countries.intermediate_region
params.metric: No derived aggregated metrics in this view; all outputs are direct column projections. Example explicit identity mappings: city_id = cities.city_id, population = cities.population.
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: join this view to a one-row-per-city dimension or fact (for example, another view keyed by city_id or a city-level dimension) on cities.city_id — safe because this view has one row per city_id so measures at the city grain are not duplicated. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to a country-level one-row-per-country view on country_code_2 or country_id if you need alternative country attributes — safe provided the country-side is one-row-per-country (this view will not duplicate because country is many-to-one from city). | Do NOT join without aggregation to one-to-many detail tables (for example: job_postings_with_company, job_skills_exploded) on city_id or country keys expecting aggregated city-level measures to remain unchanged — those joins will multiply city rows by the number of matching detail rows. If you must combine with a one-to-many table, first aggregate the one-to-many table to the city_id (or country_id) level (e.g., COUNT(*) AS postings_per_city) and then join to preserve correct counts. | Do NOT join to sibling AGG or RANK views that return multiple rows per city or per country (for example, a ranking that returns top-N per city) unless you intentionally want row multiplication; instead, re-aggregate after the join or pre-aggregate the sibling view to one row per city. | Safe join example: this_view LEFT JOIN another_city_dimension d ON cities_with_country.city_id = d.city_id — preserves one row per city. Unsafe example: this_view LEFT JOIN job_postings_with_company p ON cities_with_country.city_id = p.city_id — multiplies city rows by postings.
params.comparison: use cities_population_by_country instead when you need country-level aggregated population metrics — that sibling AGG is pre-aggregated to country grain and intended for country-level summaries, whereas cities_with_country is one row per city and contains city-level population values. | use legislator_latest_term or legislators_profile when you need legislator-specific data — those siblings focus on legislator entities and different grains (ranked or joined legislator profiles) and are unrelated in grain/purpose to city-level data. | use job_postings_with_company or job_skills_exploded when you need job-level or skill-level detail — those siblings are one-to-many with respect to cities and will multiply rows if joined directly; aggregate them first to city_id before joining to cities_with_country. | use cities_with_country rather than a raw cities table when you want country attributes joined in; prefer the raw cities table if you explicitly want to avoid any implicit country enrichment or if you need to control how missing country matches are handled.

views.description: Cities enriched with their country-level attributes (name, region, codes). Use when mapping cities to country metadata for regional analysis or currency/language join keys. | Use for: Largest cities by population in a region; Mapping cities to region/sub_region; Filter capitals or cities inserted after a date

views.name: cities_population_by_country
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  country_code_2,
  COUNT(city_id) AS city_count,
  SUM(COALESCE(population,0.0)) AS total_population_from_cities,
  AVG(COALESCE(population,0.0)) AS avg_city_population,
  MAX(COALESCE(population,0.0)) AS max_city_population,
  MIN(COALESCE(population,0.0)) AS min_city_population
FROM cities
GROUP BY country_code_2

params.description: Per-country aggregation of counts and basic population statistics computed from the cities table (one row per country_code_2).
params.when_to_use: To get the number of cities and summary population measures (sum, average, min, max) for each 2-letter country code (country_code_2). | When building country-level dashboards or reports that summarize city-level population information without joining other one-to-many details. | As a pre-aggregated source for country-level visualizations or further joins to one-row-per-country reference tables (e.g., country metadata).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to compute country population totals if the authoritative country population comes from a different table (population by country) — this view only sums populations recorded on cities and can under-count or double-count compared to country-level sources. | Do not join this view directly to another one-to-many table (for example, cities_by_region or job_postings) without re-aggregation: joining to tables that have multiple rows per country will multiply these aggregated measures and produce inflated counts/sums (aggregation/grain mismatch). | Do not use avg_city_population here as a population-weighted average of countries or regions — AVG is computed across rows in cities per country; averaging these per-country averages across countries will be misleading (cohort/aggregation mismatch). | Do not treat city_count as a distinct-city cardinality guarantee if cities.city_id is not unique or if upstream filters/joins alter city granularity; COUNT(city_id) counts non-null city_id rows in the cities table as present in the source.
params.output_schema: country_code_2: two-letter country code used as the grouping key; derived from cities.country_code_2 | city_count: number of city rows with a non-null city_id in that country; derived from COUNT(city_id) over cities.city_id | total_population_from_cities: sum of population values for cities in the country with NULL treated as 0; derived from SUM(COALESCE(cities.population, 0.0)) | avg_city_population: arithmetic mean of city population values in the country with NULL treated as 0 (AVG over COALESCE(population,0.0)); derived from AVG(COALESCE(cities.population, 0.0)) | max_city_population: maximum city population value in the country with NULL treated as 0; derived from MAX(COALESCE(cities.population, 0.0)) | min_city_population: minimum city population value in the country with NULL treated as 0; derived from MIN(COALESCE(cities.population, 0.0))
params.metric: city_count = COUNT(cities.city_id) | total_population_from_cities = SUM(COALESCE(cities.population, 0.0)) | avg_city_population = AVG(COALESCE(cities.population, 0.0)) | max_city_population = MAX(COALESCE(cities.population, 0.0)) | min_city_population = MIN(COALESCE(cities.population, 0.0))
params.composition: Safe: join to a one-row-per-country reference/view (e.g., countries, cities_with_country if it is one-row-per-country) on country_code_2 — safe because this aggregation has exactly one row per country_code_2 so measures are not duplicated. | Safe: join to sibling one-row-per-country views (if present) on country_code_2 — preserves correctness. | Not safe: do NOT join directly to cities (or any other one-to-many table keyed by country_code_2) without re-aggregating the detail side first, because the join will duplicate the aggregated country row across multiple detail rows and inflate counts/sums (aggregation duplication). | Not safe: do NOT join to job_postings_with_company, job_skills_exploded, aliens_favorites_agg, or other multi-row-per-country tables on country_code_2 unless you first aggregate those tables to the country level; otherwise city_count and total_population_from_cities will be multiplied by the number of matching detail rows. | If you need to combine this view with another table that is many-to-one into countries, prefer: (a) aggregate the many-side to country_code_2 first, then join country-to-country, or (b) join and then re-aggregate at country_code_2, to avoid mis-counts.
params.comparison: use cities_with_country instead when you need city-level columns or to preserve city granularity for downstream joins — cities_with_country is a JOIN view that retains city rows rather than aggregating to country. | use aliens_favorites_agg instead when you need aggregated favorites metrics for aliens per country — it is an AGG sibling but over a different domain and may align with social metrics rather than population. | use legislators_profile or legislator_latest_term when you need legislator-level or latest-term data tied to countries — these are JOIN/RANK views appropriate for person-level analytics, not city population aggregates. | use job_postings_with_company or job_postings_salary_rank when your analysis centers on job-level or salary-rank summaries rather than city population; those views operate at job/posting granularity and have different grain and keys. | In short: prefer sibling JOIN/RANK views when you need row-level detail or ranked/latest records; prefer this AGG view when you only need country-level city population summaries.

views.description: Aggregated population metrics per country_code_2 based on cities. Use for country-level population summaries, average city size, and ranking countries by summed city populations. | Use for: Total city population by country; Average and maximum city size per country; Countries with many recorded cities

views.name: legislator_latest_term
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  lt.id_bioguide,
  lt.term_number,
  lt.term_id,
  lt.term_type,
  lt.term_start,
  lt.term_end,
  lt.state,
  lt.district,
  lt.class,
  lt.party,
  lt.how,
  lt.url,
  lt.address,
  lt.phone,
  lt.fax,
  lt.contact_form,
  lt.office,
  lt.state_rank,
  lt.rss_url,
  lt.caucus,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY lt.id_bioguide ORDER BY lt.term_start DESC) AS term_rank
FROM legislators_terms AS lt

params.description: Provides the latest terms per legislator (ranked by term_start) with term-level attributes; answers questions about a legislator's most recent term details.
params.when_to_use: Get the most recent term(s) for each legislator (e.g., show current office details where term_start indicates recency). | Join to legislator-level profile data when you need term-specific fields (party, district, office) but want to avoid scanning all terms and computing recency manually. | Present a list of terms for a legislator ordered by recency, and pick top-ranked (term_rank = 1) as the latest.
params.when_not_to_use: Aggregating counts of related records (e.g., counting bills or votes per legislator) by joining this view to many-to-one detail tables without re-aggregation — doing so will multiply rows because those tables can be many per term. Always aggregate the many-side first or join on a deduplicated key. | Using this view as if it were a single-row-per-legislator canonical profile without filtering term_rank = 1 — the view returns one row per term_id and assigns a rank per legislator; treating it as single-row-per-legislator will return multiple rows (one per term). | Joining to other term-level or event tables that are at a finer grain (e.g., daily events, multiple contacts) expecting measures to be preserved — such joins can duplicate term rows and thus duplicate any derived counts unless you re-aggregate or join on a deduplicated key. | Relying on term_rank alone to define "current" membership if term_end semantics differ (NULL vs future date) — term_rank orders by term_start only, not by term_end or whether a term is active.
params.output_schema: id_bioguide: Legislator identifier (source: legislators_terms.id_bioguide) | term_number: Term sequence/number for this legislator (source: legislators_terms.term_number) | term_id: Primary identifier of the term row (source: legislators_terms.term_id) | term_type: Type of term (e.g., 'senate' or 'house') (source: legislators_terms.term_type) | term_start: Start datetime/date of the term (source: legislators_terms.term_start) | term_end: End datetime/date of the term (source: legislators_terms.term_end) | state: State associated with the term (source: legislators_terms.state) | district: District associated with the term (source: legislators_terms.district) | class: Senate class where applicable (source: legislators_terms.class) | party: Party affiliation for the term (source: legislators_terms.party) | how: How the legislator obtained the term (e.g., election, appointment) (source: legislators_terms.how) | url: Term-level URL (source: legislators_terms.url) | address: Term-level office address (source: legislators_terms.address) | phone: Term-level phone number (source: legislators_terms.phone) | fax: Term-level fax number (source: legislators_terms.fax) | contact_form: Term-level contact form URL (source: legislators_terms.contact_form) | office: Office identifier/name for the term (source: legislators_terms.office) | state_rank: Rank within the state for the term (source: legislators_terms.state_rank) | rss_url: Term-level RSS feed URL (source: legislators_terms.rss_url) | caucus: Caucus membership for the term (source: legislators_terms.caucus) | term_rank: Rank of the term per legislator, computed as RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY id_bioguide ORDER BY term_start DESC) (source: computed)
params.grounded_columns: legislators_terms.id_bioguide | legislators_terms.term_number | legislators_terms.term_id | legislators_terms.term_type | legislators_terms.term_start | legislators_terms.term_end | legislators_terms.state | legislators_terms.district | legislators_terms.class | legislators_terms.party | legislators_terms.how | legislators_terms.url | legislators_terms.address | legislators_terms.phone | legislators_terms.fax | legislators_terms.contact_form | legislators_terms.office | legislators_terms.state_rank | legislators_terms.rss_url | legislators_terms.caucus
params.metric: term_rank = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY legislators_terms.id_bioguide ORDER BY legislators_terms.term_start DESC)
params.composition: Safe to join (one-to-one or many-to-one): join this view to a legislator-level profile or dimension keyed by id_bioguide (e.g., legislators_profile) on id_bioguide — safe because for a given term_id row this view is one row and joining to one-row-per-legislator preserves cardinality for that term row. | Safe pattern: SELECT ... FROM legislator_latest_term lt JOIN legislators_profile p ON lt.id_bioguide = p.id_bioguide WHERE lt.term_rank = 1; — this preserves term-level granularity and will not duplicate term rows because legislators_profile is one-row-per-legislator. | Do NOT join directly to many-row tables (e.g., votes, bills, office_visits, or any exploded skill/job_postings tables) without aggregating the many-side first. Example anti-pattern: joining legislator_latest_term to a 'bills' table that has many bills per term_id will multiply the legislator_latest_term row for each bill, inflating counts or duplicating term attributes. Instead aggregate bills per term_id first (e.g., COUNT(*) GROUP BY term_id) and then join on term_id. | Do NOT rely on joining by id_bioguide alone to tables that are term-scoped (e.g., term-specific events) unless you also join on term_id or re-aggregate by term_id, because joining only on id_bioguide can merge events from different terms into the same term row. | If you need one canonical row per legislator, filter WHERE term_rank = 1 in this view before further joins or use a sibling view that is explicitly one-row-per-legislator.
params.comparison: use legislators_profile instead when you need a single row per legislator (one-row-per-id_bioguide) containing profile-level attributes and you do not need term-specific fields — legislators_profile is a join-style sibling intended for profile consolidation. | use job_postings_salary_rank, job_skills_exploded, or other AGG/JOIN siblings when you need specialized derived metrics (ranking or exploded many-to-one relationships) for those domains — they are structured for their domain-specific grains. Do not substitute this view for those because this view's grain is term_id (term-level), not job or skill-level. | This view differs from legislators_profile (JOIN) in that it is term-grained (one row per term_id with a per-legislator term_rank) rather than one row per legislator. Choose this view when term attributes and recency ordering are required; choose legislators_profile when you need deduplicated legislator-level attributes.

views.description: Latest term per legislator ordered by term_start. Exposes a term_rank so callers can filter rank = 1 for the most recent term. Useful for current office holder, current party, state, or district lookups. | Use for: Who is the current legislator for a given bioguide or state/district; Current party or office for each legislator; Filter to most recent term per legislator

views.name: legislators_profile
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  l.id_bioguide,
  l.full_name,
  l.first_name,
  l.last_name,
  l.middle_name,
  l.nickname,
  l.suffix,
  l.birthday,
  l.gender,
  l.id_govtrack,
  l.id_icpsr,
  l.id_wikipedia,
  l.id_wikidata,
  l.id_opensecrets,
  lt.term_id AS term_id,
  lt.term_start AS term_start,
  lt.term_end AS term_end,
  lt.term_type AS term_type,
  lt.state AS state,
  lt.district AS district,
  lt.party AS party
FROM legislators AS l
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT * FROM legislators_terms
) AS lt
  ON l.id_bioguide = lt.id_bioguide
  AND lt.term_start = (
    SELECT MAX(term_start) FROM legislators_terms AS lt2 WHERE lt2.id_bioguide = l.id_bioguide
  )

params.description: Provides one-row-per-legislator (id_bioguide) enriched with that legislator's most-recent term attributes (term_id, term_start, term_end, term_type, state, district, party) as of the latest term_start in legislators_terms.
params.when_to_use: Look up a legislator's identifying fields and biographical IDs along with the most-recent (latest term_start) term information. | Display a profile card or directory row for each legislator showing their current/most-recent office, state, district and party. | Join to dimension tables keyed at the legislator level (for example to fetch photos or demographics stored one-per-legislator) without changing cardinality.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use as a time-series or historical-term table when you need all terms for a legislator — this view intentionally returns only the row(s) matching the maximum term_start per legislator. | Do not aggregate counts of terms or compute metrics like total terms served — because the view already filters to the latest term, aggregating here will undercount or misrepresent historical totals. | Do not rely on this view to return a single row per legislator if legislators have identical term_start values for multiple concurrent records — in that edge case the LEFT JOIN may return multiple rows per id_bioguide (see anti-pattern below). | Do not join one-to-many event/activity tables (for example votes or bill sponsorships) directly to this view and then sum counts without first re-aggregating the many-side — that will produce inflated counts because this view is one-row-per-legislator-with-latest-term while the other table is many-per-legislator.
params.output_schema: id_bioguide: the legislator's bioguide identifier; source = legislators.id_bioguide | full_name: full display name of the legislator; source = legislators.full_name | first_name: source = legislators.first_name | last_name: source = legislators.last_name | middle_name: source = legislators.middle_name | nickname: source = legislators.nickname | suffix: name suffix (e.g., Jr.); source = legislators.suffix | birthday: date of birth; source = legislators.birthday | gender: source = legislators.gender | id_govtrack: external govtrack id; source = legislators.id_govtrack | id_icpsr: external ICPSR id; source = legislators.id_icpsr | id_wikipedia: wikipedia id/username; source = legislators.id_wikipedia | id_wikidata: wikidata identifier; source = legislators.id_wikidata | id_opensecrets: OpenSecrets id; source = legislators.id_opensecrets | term_id: identifier of the latest term for this legislator as chosen by MAX(term_start); source = legislators_terms.term_id (via lt.term_id) | term_start: start date of that latest term = lt.term_start (the MAX(term_start) per id_bioguide) | term_end: end date of that latest term; source = legislators_terms.term_end (via lt.term_end) | term_type: type/category of the term (e.g., 'senate'/'house'); source = legislators_terms.term_type (via lt.term_type) | state: state for that latest term; source = legislators_terms.state (via lt.state) | district: district for that latest term; source = legislators_terms.district (via lt.district) | party: party for that latest term; source = legislators_terms.party (via lt.party)
params.grounded_columns: legislators.id_bioguide | legislators.full_name | legislators.first_name | legislators.last_name | legislators.middle_name | legislators.nickname | legislators.suffix | legislators.birthday | legislators.gender | legislators.id_govtrack | legislators.id_icpsr | legislators.id_wikipedia | legislators.id_wikidata | legislators.id_opensecrets | legislators_terms.term_id | legislators_terms.id_bioguide | legislators_terms.term_start | legislators_terms.term_end | legislators_terms.term_type | legislators_terms.state | legislators_terms.district | legislators_terms.party
params.metric: term_start_latest = MAX(legislators_terms.term_start) FILTER (PARTITION BY legislators_terms.id_bioguide) — implemented in the view by correlating lt.term_start with (SELECT MAX(term_start) FROM legislators_terms AS lt2 WHERE lt2.id_bioguide = l.id_bioguide) | latest_term_fields = the set {term_id, term_start, term_end, term_type, state, district, party} selected from legislators_terms for rows where term_start = term_start_latest per id_bioguide
params.composition: Safe to join (one-to-one or many-to-one) on legislators.id_bioguide to tables/views that are also one-row-per-legislator (for example a hypothetical 'legislator_photos' with primary key id_bioguide). Join on id_bioguide — safe because this view returns at most one row per legislator id in the normal case. | Safe to join to small lookup/dimension tables keyed by state, party or term_type using the state/party/term_type columns — these are many-to-one from this view's perspective and will not duplicate rows if the dimension is one-row-per-key. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables keyed by id_bioguide (for example votes, bill_sponsorships, social_media_posts) without pre-aggregating those tables to one-row-per-id_bioguide; doing so will multiply rows and any aggregates derived after the join will be inflated. | Do NOT join to legislators_terms (or another term-level table) without restricting/aggregating first — joining the full legislators_terms would reintroduce all historical terms and would produce multiple rows per legislator, defeating this view's latest-term intent. | If you must combine with a many-side (for example to compute total_votes_per_legislator), first aggregate the many-side to one row per id_bioguide (e.g., SELECT id_bioguide, COUNT(*) AS votes FROM votes GROUP BY id_bioguide) and then LEFT JOIN to this view on id_bioguide.
params.comparison: use legislator_latest_term (RANK) instead when you need deterministic tie-breaking for cases where multiple terms have the same term_start — the RANK-based view likely provides a single-row selection policy (e.g., ROW_NUMBER or RANK with ordering) and can avoid returning multiple rows when MAX(term_start) is not unique. | use a fully historical terms view (not listed but implied) or directly query legislators_terms when you need all terms or to compute metrics across all terms (e.g., total terms served, term-length aggregates). | do not use this view as a substitute for an aggregation view (e.g., aliens_favorites_agg style) when you require counts or sums — this view contains no pre-computed aggregates.

views.description: Legislator master rows with their most-recent term attributes (party, state, district) by joining to the latest term. Use for person-level queries that need current office info alongside biographical identifiers. | Use for: List legislators with current state and party; Join legislator biographical info to current office attributes; Filter legislators by party or state

views.name: alien_profiles
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  a.id,
  a.first_name,
  a.last_name,
  a.email,
  a.gender,
  a.type,
  a.birth_year AS birth_year,
  ad.age AS age,
  ad.favorite_food AS favorite_food,
  ad.feeding_frequency AS feeding_frequency,
  ad.aggressive AS aggressive,
  al.current_location AS current_location,
  al.state AS state,
  al.country AS country,
  al.occupation AS occupation
FROM aliens AS a
LEFT JOIN alien_data AS ad
  ON a.id = ad.id
LEFT JOIN aliens_location AS al
  ON ad.current_location = al.current_location

params.description: Provides one-row-per-alien profile combining core alien table, supplemental alien_data, and location details — useful for profile-level queries and lookups.
params.when_to_use: Look up full profile attributes for a single alien id or a list of alien ids (e.g., display a profile card). | Produce reporting that needs non-aggregated profile attributes (name, contact, demographics, occupation, favorite food, etc.) at the alien-grain. | Join this view to other one-row-per-entity datasets (e.g., events keyed by alien id) when you need profile attributes attached to each event row without aggregation.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to answer aggregated/historical questions (e.g., counts of aliens by city or average feeding_frequency per city) without first aggregating — the view is row-grain and contains no GROUP BY; using it directly in aggregations may miscount if joined to many-to-one/many-to-many tables. | Do not assume feed-frequency or age are time-stamped or the latest if alien_data contains multiple rows per id; this SQL LEFT JOINs alien_data ON a.id = ad.id without de-duplication, so if alien_data has multiple rows per id it could produce duplicate rows or arbitrary one-to-many multiplicity depending on the underlying DB engine and data. | Do not join to aliens_location using a.id = al.id — this view joins aliens_location ON ad.current_location = al.current_location. If you instead join on location keys incorrectly, you may introduce mismatches or duplicate rows. | Avoid using this view as the source of metrics that expect strictly normalized cardinality (e.g., sum of a metric stored per-alien) after joining additional one-to-many tables without re-aggregation — that will multiply alien rows and produce silently-wrong totals.
params.output_schema: id: Unique identifier for the alien profile — sourced from aliens.id. | first_name: Alien's first name string — sourced from aliens.first_name. | last_name: Alien's last name string — sourced from aliens.last_name. | email: Contact/email for the alien — sourced from aliens.email. | gender: Gender attribute for the alien — sourced from aliens.gender. | type: Alien type/category — sourced from aliens.type. | birth_year: Birth year of the alien (raw column) — sourced from aliens.birth_year (aliased as birth_year). | age: Age value from supplemental data — sourced from alien_data.age (aliased as age). | favorite_food: Favorite food from supplemental data — sourced from alien_data.favorite_food (aliased as favorite_food). | feeding_frequency: Feeding frequency metric from supplemental data — sourced from alien_data.feeding_frequency (aliased as feeding_frequency). | aggressive: Aggression flag/indicator from supplemental data — sourced from alien_data.aggressive (aliased as aggressive). | current_location: Location identifier referenced in alien_data — sourced from aliens_location.current_location via the join from alien_data.current_location. | state: State name/identifier for the current location — sourced from aliens_location.state (aliased as state). | country: Country name/identifier for the current location — sourced from aliens_location.country (aliased as country). | occupation: Occupation at the current location — sourced from aliens_location.occupation (aliased as occupation).
params.grounded_columns: aliens.id | aliens.first_name | aliens.last_name | aliens.email | aliens.gender | aliens.type | aliens.birth_year | alien_data.id | alien_data.age | alien_data.favorite_food | alien_data.feeding_frequency | alien_data.aggressive | alien_data.current_location | aliens_location.current_location | aliens_location.state | aliens_location.country | aliens_location.occupation
params.metric: This view exposes no aggregated metrics. All outputs are direct columns or 1:1 lookups. (No derived aggregate expressions present.)
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE joins: You may safely join this view to a one-row-per-alien table or view on aliens.id (e.g., an events table already scoped to one event per alien) because alien_profiles is defined at the grain of aliens.id — joining a single extra row per id preserves row-level measures. | Cardinality-SAFE join guidance example: join to a confirmed_one_row_per_alien_view ON alien_profiles.id = confirmed_one_row_per_alien_view.id — safe because both sides are one row per alien id. | Do NOT join without care to one-to-many tables such as an interactions table (many interactions per alien) or any exploded skill/education tables, unless you aggregate the many-side first. Otherwise the profile row will be duplicated for each matching many-side row and counts/sums derived from this view will be multiplied. | Do NOT join to aliens_location on aliens.id (i.e., aliases that imply a join key mismatch) — this view uses aliens_location via alien_data.current_location = aliens_location.current_location. If you join differently you risk mismatches or duplicate rows if multiple locations share the same identifier or if keys are not unique. | If alien_data is not guaranteed unique per aliens.id (multiple rows per id), this view risks producing multiple rows per alien. To compose safely with other data, ensure alien_data is pre-aggregated or deduplicated (e.g., latest_by_ts or row_number = 1) before joining, or replace the LEFT JOIN with a subquery that selects one row per id.
params.comparison: use aliens_favorites_agg instead when you need aggregated metrics about favorite_food or feeding_frequency across groups (it is an AGG view) — alien_profiles is row-level and will return one record per alien rather than group-level aggregates. | use legislators_profile or legislator_latest_term when working with legislator entities — they are sibling views for legislators and are architected for that domain; alien_profiles is specific to alien entity tables. | use cities_with_country or cities_population_by_country for city- or country-level geography aggregations — alien_profiles only enriches each alien with a current_location and location attributes, but does not provide population-level aggregations. | use job_postings_with_company or job_skills_exploded when your analysis concerns job postings or skills; those sibling views are shaped for job-related joins/aggregations whereas alien_profiles is a person-profile join.

views.description: Alien profile view combining base aliens table with denormalized demographic/location/details present in alien_data, aliens_location, and aliens_details when keys align. Useful for analyses that need full profile attributes for each alien. | Use for: Profiles of aliens including location and aggression flag; Count aliens by favorite_food or feeding_frequency; Filter aliens by region/country/state or occupation

views.name: aliens_favorites_agg
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  COALESCE(favorite_food, '') AS favorite_food,
  COALESCE(feeding_frequency, '') AS feeding_frequency,
  COUNT(id) AS alien_count,
  SUM(COALESCE(aggressive,0)) AS aggressive_count,
  CASE WHEN COUNT(id) = 0 THEN 0.0 ELSE SUM(COALESCE(aggressive,0)) * 1.0 / COUNT(id) END AS aggressive_rate
FROM alien_data
GROUP BY favorite_food, feeding_frequency

params.description: Counts of aliens by their favorite_food and feeding_frequency, with number and share that are marked aggressive.
params.when_to_use: Aggregating population-level counts and aggressive proportions broken down by favorite_food and feeding_frequency. | Creating reports or charts that compare how common each favorite_food × feeding_frequency combination is and the fraction that are aggressive. | Filtering or slicing by favorite_food or feeding_frequency to show counts and aggressive rate for those groups.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view to row-level alien tables and assuming results remain row-level — doing so will duplicate counts because this view is already aggregated (grain is favorite_food × feeding_frequency). | Attempting to calculate per-alien metrics (for example, selecting individual alien attributes) from this view — it has aggregated counts, not individual rows, so you cannot get unique alien ids from it. | Treating aggressive_rate as a valid measure to average across other arbitrary groupings without re-aggregation — averaging rates from multiple rows will produce incorrect results unless weighted by alien_count. | Using this view to answer time-cohort questions (e.g., changes over time) — it contains no time dimension and so cannot support cohort/time-based trends.
params.output_schema: favorite_food: favorite_food value (string). Derived from base column alien_data.favorite_food; NULLs normalized to empty string by COALESCE. | feeding_frequency: feeding_frequency value (string). Derived from base column alien_data.feeding_frequency; NULLs normalized to empty string by COALESCE. | alien_count: count of alien rows in alien_data for the favorite_food × feeding_frequency combination. Defined as COUNT(id) in the SQL; id is from alien_data.id. | aggressive_count: sum of the aggressive flag for the group. Defined as SUM(COALESCE(aggressive, 0)) where aggressive is a base column alien_data.aggressive (assumed numeric/boolean represented as 1/0). NULL aggressive values are treated as 0. | aggressive_rate: proportion aggressive in the group. Defined as aggressive_count * 1.0 / alien_count when alien_count > 0, else 0.0. Expressed in SQL as CASE WHEN COUNT(id) = 0 THEN 0.0 ELSE SUM(COALESCE(aggressive,0)) * 1.0 / COUNT(id) END.
params.metric: alien_count = COUNT(alien_data.id) | aggressive_count = SUM(COALESCE(alien_data.aggressive, 0)) | aggressive_rate = CASE WHEN COUNT(alien_data.id) = 0 THEN 0.0 ELSE SUM(COALESCE(alien_data.aggressive,0)) * 1.0 / COUNT(alien_data.id) END
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE: join to a dimension that is one-row-per-favorite_food (or one-row-per-feeding_frequency) on favorite_food (or feeding_frequency) respectively — safe because this view has one row per favorite_food×feeding_frequency and joining to a one-to-one dimension will not duplicate aggregated measures. | cardinality-SAFE: join to a canned lookup of favorite_food attributes (e.g., food_descriptions) on favorite_food — safe if that lookup is one-row-per-favorite_food. | DO NOT join this view to any table or view that is one-to-many relative to the view's grain (e.g., join to alien_profiles or any row-level alien table) without re-aggregation. Joining to a row-level alien table on favorite_food and/or feeding_frequency will multiply this view's aggregated counts by the number of matching alien_profile rows, producing duplicated/incorrect measures. | If you need to combine with another multi-row aggregation (for example, counts by city), align on a common grain and re-aggregate after join (use weighted averages for rates: combined_rate = SUM(aggressive_count) / SUM(alien_count)). | When joining to sibling JOIN-type views that are row-level (e.g., alien_profiles JOIN), instead bring the join into the source aggregation (recompute counts from row-level) rather than joining this aggregated view to them.
params.comparison: use alien_profiles (JOIN) instead when you need row-level attributes or to filter before aggregation — alien_profiles contains individual alien rows and should be aggregated to exactly the desired grain to avoid mismatch. | use cities_population_by_country (AGG) when your analysis requires aggregation by geographic dimensions (country/city) rather than by favorite_food × feeding_frequency; cities_population_by_country has a geographic aggregation grain and is appropriate for population by place. | use legislator_latest_term (RANK) or job_postings_salary_rank (RANK) when you need rank/ordering semantics rather than simple counts and proportions — those sibling RANK views implement window/ranking logic which is different from this simple group aggregate.

views.description: Counts and aggression rates grouped by favorite_food and feeding_frequency. Useful for summaries of preferences and behavior among alien cohorts. | Use for: Which foods are associated with higher aggression?; Counts of aliens by feeding frequency; Compare aggression rates between feeding_frequency cohorts

views.name: job_postings_salary_rank
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  job_id,
  company_id,
  job_country,
  job_title_short,
  salary_year_avg,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY job_country ORDER BY salary_year_avg DESC) AS salary_rank
FROM job_postings_fact

params.description: Provides, at the job_postings (job_id) grain, the average annual salary per job and the within-country rank of that salary (1 = highest salary in that country).
params.when_to_use: Ranking jobs within each country by their average annual salary. | Reporting or filtering top-N job postings by salary within a specified country. | Displaying salary information alongside job-level attributes where each row represents a single job posting.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly to tables that expand job_postings (e.g., skills, multiple contacts) expecting aggregated totals — doing so will produce duplicated job rows and therefore incorrect ranks/metrics because the view is at job_id grain. | Using this view to answer company-level or country-level aggregated questions (e.g., average salary per company or per country) without re-aggregation — the view contains one row per job, not an aggregate for the company or country. | Mixing cohorts incorrectly: computing time-based cohorts or period-over-period comparisons by joining to a time series without first aggregating by job_id and period — rank is computed across all rows in job_postings_fact as present, so cohort-based ranks require recomputing rank per cohort. | Assuming salary_rank is stable after joining to one-to-many siblings (e.g., job_skills_exploded) — those joins duplicate rows and will lead to duplicated appearances of the same job and can mislead counts and downstream aggregations unless de-duplicated or re-aggregated.
params.output_schema: job_id: unique identifier of the job posting at job_postings_fact.job_id; this view is one row per job_id (grain). | company_id: identifier of the company posting the job, taken from job_postings_fact.company_id (no aggregation). | job_country: country code/name for the job posting, taken from job_postings_fact.job_country (partition key for ranking). | job_title_short: short job title string from job_postings_fact.job_title_short (no aggregation). | salary_year_avg: average annual salary for that job as provided by job_postings_fact.salary_year_avg (base numeric metric, not recomputed here). | salary_rank: integer rank of salary_year_avg within the same job_country computed with RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY job_country ORDER BY salary_year_avg DESC). Ties receive the same rank and gaps may occur.
params.metric: salary_year_avg = job_postings_fact.salary_year_avg | salary_rank = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY job_postings_fact.job_country ORDER BY job_postings_fact.salary_year_avg DESC)
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to one-row-per-company or one-row-per-country dimensions on their keys without changing measures — e.g., join to a company dimension on company_id (safe because company dimension is one-row-per-company and will not duplicate job rows). | Safe: join to cities_with_country on job_country (assuming cities_with_country is one-row-per-country in your catalog) if that view indeed provides one row per country; this will not duplicate job rows or alter salary_rank. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables/views such as job_skills_exploded or any exploded/skill-level view without first aggregating or deduplicating back to job_id — those joins will produce multiple rows per job_id and effectively duplicate salary_year_avg and the job-level row, which corrupts counts, sums, and can mislead downstream aggregations. | If you must join to one-to-many data (e.g., skills), either: (a) aggregate the one-to-many side to one row per job_id before joining (for example, collect skills into an array or compute counts), or (b) join and then re-aggregate at the job_id level and recompute any ranks/aggregates as needed. | Do NOT rely on salary_rank remaining meaningful after arbitrary joins that change the rowset; the rank was computed over the set of job_postings_fact rows as selected by this view and should be recomputed if the partitioning set changes (e.g., filtering to a subset of jobs or joining that filters rows).
params.comparison: Use job_postings_with_company instead when you need company dimension attributes joined inline and you want those descriptive fields resolved in the same step; job_postings_with_company performs joins to company data rather than only exposing company_id. | Use job_skills_exploded when you need a row per job-skill pair (one-to-many) — but note that job_skills_exploded expands job rows and is not suitable when you require one row per job (this view). | Use cities_population_by_country when you need country-level population aggregates (this view is job-level and will require aggregation to country level for meaningful composition). | Use legislator_latest_term, legislators_profile, alien_profiles, aliens_favorites_agg, legislation_calendar when working in those domains — they are sibling views for different entities; prefer them if you need their specific domain-level aggregations/ranks rather than job-level salary ranks.

views.description: Rank job postings within each country by salary_year_avg (descending). Exposes salary_rank to let downstream queries pick top-N jobs per country or filter by rank ranges. | Use for: Top paid jobs per country; Identify percentile or rank of a specific job's salary within its country

views.name: legislation_calendar
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  date,
  month_name,
  day_of_month
FROM legislation_date_dim

params.description: A normalized calendar view that provides one row per date with simple date attributes (month name and day of month).
params.when_to_use: When you need a date dimension keyed by exact calendar date for reporting or joining to fact tables by date. | When you need to display or filter on human-friendly date attributes such as month name or day-of-month.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly to a one-to-many fact without ensuring the fact is the multiplicative side — doing so is fine if the fact is the many side, but using this view as if it were aggregated (for example, summing values from this view) is wrong because this view is strictly a date dimension (grain = one row per date) and contains no aggregated metrics. | Using this view to represent time ranges, cohorts, or fiscal periods beyond the explicit date-level attributes provided — it only carries calendar date, month_name, and day_of_month and does not encode fiscal weeks/quarters or cohort/window definitions. | Assuming uniqueness beyond the 'date' column (for example, grouping by month_name alone to represent a month-level grain) without explicit aggregation — month_name repeats across multiple rows and would require aggregation to produce month-level metrics.
params.output_schema: date: the unique calendar date for the row; derived directly from legislation_date_dim.date | month_name: the calendar month name (e.g., 'January'); derived directly from legislation_date_dim.month_name | day_of_month: integer day of the month (1-31); derived directly from legislation_date_dim.day_of_month
params.metric: No derived metrics or aggregates are defined in this view. All output columns are direct projections from legislation_date_dim. (No expressions/aggregations)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to fact tables or event tables on fact.event_date = legislation_calendar.date — safe because legislation_calendar has one row per date, so joining a many-row fact to this one-row-per-date dimension does NOT duplicate the fact's measures (the fact remains the multiplicative side). | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to other one-row-per-date or one-row-per-key date dimensions (if present) on date — safe because both sides are one-to-one on date. | Do NOT join this view to a one-to-many dimension (for example, a table that explodes a date into multiple cohort buckets per date) without re-aggregating first, because doing so will multiply rows and silently inflate any measures calculated after the join. | Do NOT join this view to a many-to-one table and then assume aggregated results from this view alone; always perform aggregation on the multiplicative side after joining (for example, sum values on the fact table grouped by legislation_calendar.date). | Examples: Safe — JOIN fact_table f ON f.date = legislation_calendar.date (aggregate f metrics after join). Unsafe — JOIN legislation_calendar to job_skills_exploded (if job_skills_exploded has multiple rows per date) and then SUM(1) from legislation_calendar expecting unique counts.
params.comparison: use legislator_latest_term instead when you need legislator term-level data (legislator_latest_term has ranked, term-specific columns) — legislation_calendar is only a date dimension and does not contain legislator or term information. | use cities_population_by_country when you need aggregated population metrics by country (cities_population_by_country is an aggregated view) — legislation_calendar provides only date attributes, not any aggregated demographic metrics. | use job_postings_with_company or job_postings_salary_rank when you require job-posting-level records or salary ranking logic — those sibling views join or rank job-posting data, whereas legislation_calendar only provides date attributes for joining or filtering by date.

views.description: Normalized date dimension for legislation-related dates exposing date components. Use for joining and filtering by month/day when analyzing legislation timelines. | Use for: Aggregate events by month or day from legislation-related datasets; Filter records by month_name or day_of_month
